Four further buttons, Images, Fonts, Sounds and Music, open the operating system's file manager on the folders for those game assets. This makes it easy for the user to copy and paste new game assets into the right place.

The standard Python3 mode (see below) is probably a better environment for more advanced pygame-only development. Nu ensures that all the game assets required by the Pygame Zero introductory tutorial are available by default.

docs.title: Standard Python3 Mode
docs.text:
This mode is for creating simple Python 3 programs. As with the other modes, there is a REPL for live programming, but in this case it is an iPython based REPL that uses project Jupyter. As with other Jupyter notebooks, it's possible to embed graphics and charts into the REPL so it becomes a interesting to read and work with.

There are two ways to run your script in this mode:

  1. Click the "Run" button: will launch the script using Python's interactive mode (so you'll be dropped into a basic interactive Python shell upon the script's completion). A script that lists the packages it needs in a PEP 723 # /// script block is run with uv run instead, which fetches them first (and can't drop into the shell).
  2. Click the "Debug" button: Python mode transitions to the debug mode - a graphical way to inspect and watch your code execute.

Because of the overhead needed to start the graphical debugger it takes longer to start running your script. This is especially noticeable on the Raspberry Pi.

Python 2 isn't supported by Nu and never will be.

docs.title: Debug Mode
docs.text:
It's only possible to enter debug mode from standard Python mode. It's purpose is to manage the execution and inspection of your code.

Clicking the margin of the editor toggles "break points" that tell the debugger where to pause. Once paused it's possible to inspect the state of various objects at that moment in the code's execution and step over, into and out of lines of code. You're able to watch Python execute your code, allowing you to discover where there may be bugs.

Once the code has finished the debug mode transitions back to standard Python mode.

docs.title: Create a New Mode
docs.text:
A new mode is a plugin: a Python package with a mu.plugins entry point, whose mode class subclasses mu.plugin.Mode (or mu.plugin.MicroPythonMode for a board with a serial REPL) and which imports nothing from Nu except mu.plugin. Writing a Nu plugin is the contract; this section is about the mode itself. Start from the template in plugins/example/, and use the two bundled plugins as worked examples:

  • Pygame Zero (plugins/pygamezero/nu_pygamezero/mode.py) runs the learner's program in their Python environment, toggles a toolbar button while it runs, opens folders, puts demo files in the workspace and needs packages in the learner's environment.
  • CircuitPython (plugins/circuitpython/nu_circuitpython/mode.py) is a MicroPythonMode: it recognises its boards when they're plugged in, keeps the learner's files on the board's drive, and gets Serial and Plotter buttons that talk to the board's REPL.

The core's own two modes, Python 3 and the Debugger (mu/modes/python3.py and mu/modes/debugger.py), are the exception: they're built in, registered in setup_modes in mu/app.py, and use Nu's internals directly. Don't add another mode that way.

docs.title: Create a Class
docs.text:
The most important aspects of a mode are encapsulated in a class that represents the mode. It must inherit from mu.plugin.Mode (Nu's BaseMode). If your new mode is for a MicroPython based device, inherit from mu.plugin.MicroPythonMode instead, since this includes various helpful utilities for such things as finding a connected device and running a REPL over a USB-serial connection.

The convention is a module of its own for the mode, next to the plugin that registers it. For example, the Pygame Zero plugin's nu_pygamezero/mode.py holds the PyGameZeroMode class, and nu_pygamezero/__init__.py the PygameZeroPlugin that registers it.

docs.title: Integrate the Mode
docs.text:
Nu needs to know that the new mode is available to use. A plugin does this in two steps:

  • Register the mode from the plugin: a ModePlugin with mode = YourMode does it for you (and images registers the folder of icons your mode uses).
  • Advertise the plugin with a mu.plugins entry point in your package's pyproject.toml, and install the package into the environment Nu runs from. Nu finds it the next time it starts.

Nu creates the mode with its internal editor and view objects and sets self.host to the Host that registered it. Reach the editor through self.host: self.editor and self.view are internal and can change in any release.

docs.title: Update the Class's Behaviour
docs.text:
The core elements of your new mode's class that need updating include some attributes and three methods.

The attributes that must be changed are:

  • name -- the full name of the mode, for example, "Pygame Zero".
  • short_name -- a stable, unique id, used as a key in the settings and saved sessions. Don't change it once people use your mode.
  • description -- a short description of the mode to be displayed in the mode picker. For example, "Make games with Pygame Zero".
  • icon -- an icon used to represent the mode in the mode picker: the name of a .png (or .svg) image in your plugin's registered images folder (or one of Nu's own in mu/resources/images).

Additional attributes with safe default values set in the Mode class which may be of value for you to change are:

  • save_timeout -- the number of seconds to wait before auto-saving work. If this value is 0 (zero) Nu will not auto-save changed files when in this mode (CircuitPython sets it: a board restarts whenever a file on it is saved).
  • builtins -- a list of strings defining symbols that Nu's code checker must assume are builtins (above and beyond Python's standard builtins).
  • star_imports -- a dict mapping a module to the names its import * brings in (the micro:bit lists from microbit import *'s). The code checker reads such an import as naming them, so it can still spot undefined names.
  • module_names -- the module names the learner mustn't use for their own files, because they'd hide a real module (CircuitPython lists the modules built into CircuitPython).
  • uses_user_environment -- set it to True if the mode runs the learner's programs in Nu's Python environment, so the admin dialog shows that environment's variables and third-party packages.

A mode may also override ensure_workspace_assets(workspace_dir), which Nu calls the first time the mode is used in a session (including the mode Nu starts in) to put what it needs into the workspace (Pygame Zero creates its images, fonts, sounds and music folders with the tutorials' demo files). It must leave anything already there alone.

Note

When creating strings that will be seen by users please remember to use the conventions for internationalization (i18n). Put simply, enclose your strings in a call to _ like this:

_('This string will be translated automatically')

Please see translations for more details. (Only the bundled plugins' strings are translated today: they share Nu's catalog.)

You should pay attention to three methods of your class: actions, api and workspace_dir. You must override actions and api (see below) and may want to override workspace_dir.

The purpose of the workspace_dir method is to return a string representation of the path to the directory containing the code created with this mode. The default implementation is generally safe to use, but a board that stores the learner's code on itself may want to point to the connected device (if attached) or a safe default on the user's filesystem (if no device is attached). See how the CircuitPython mode does it. If in doubt, just use the inherited method.

However, you must override the actions method. It must return a list of dictionaries that describe the buttons to be added to Nu's user interface. Each dictionary must contain the following key/value pairs:

  • name -- the name of the button, which doubles as the name of its icon (in your plugin's images folder, or one of Nu's) and as its id, so it must be unique. Prefix your own icons' names with your plugin's name (the CircuitPython mode's Serial button is circuitpython-serial). To create a new button start with the blank button.png image in mu/resources/images and use either an icon from the FontAwesome set of icons, or some other graphical device that looks visually similar. Make sure that the colour of the image is correct blue of (hex value) #336699. Please remember to centre it within the button and make sure it has the same sort of scale as the existing buttons.
  • display_name -- the string displayed immediately underneath the button in Nu's user interface.
  • description -- the string displayed as a tool-top when the mouse pointer hovers over the button, but the button remains unclicked.
  • handler -- a reference to a method you have created in your mode's class that is called, with an event object, when the button is clicked.
  • shortcut -- a string representation of the keyboard shortcut for the button. Valid examples include, 'F5' (for function key 5) or, 'Ctrl+Shift+I' (for control-shift-I).

By way of illustration, here's the list of dictionaries returned in the CircuitPython mode. It only offers a Plotter button when Nu can show the plotter, and that button uses Nu's own plotter icon:

buttons = [
    {
        "name": "circuitpython-serial",
        "display_name": _("Serial"),
        "description": _("Open a serial connection to your device."),
        "handler": self.toggle_repl,
        "shortcut": "CTRL+Shift+U",
    }
]
if self.host.plotter_available:
    buttons.append(
        {
            "name": "plotter",
            "display_name": _("Plotter"),
            "description": _("Plot incoming REPL data."),
            "handler": self.toggle_plotter,
            "shortcut": "CTRL+Shift+P",
        }
    )
return buttons

Notice how the handlers are references to methods of the mode (here, toggle_repl and toggle_plotter come with MicroPythonMode); the details of your own are left to you. Nu simply calls the handler and expects the author of the mode to know what they're doing. Errors in handlers are reported to the learner rather than crashing Nu (see plugins).

Interactions with the editor go through self.host, the mu.plugin.Host that registered the mode: showing messages, the current tab, saving it, running the learner's program, changing a toolbar button, and so on. Its methods are listed in plugins, and its docstrings are in the api reference.

Finally, you must also override the api method, whose role is to provide a list of strings that conform to Scintilla's protocol for defining and documenting API's to be used with autocomplete and call-tips. The protocol is:

'foo.bar(arg1, args2="baz") \nMulti line\n\nEnglish description.`

Happily, various scripts in the utils directory can be used, cloned and modified to autogenerate this documentation from source code. The reason the extraction of such API related information is automated is so it makes it very quick and easy to revise such data as APIs change in the future.

Take a look at the pgzero_api.py file and you'll find a simple recipe for extracting such information from Python modules. Three modules for Python's standard library (json, inspect and importlib) are used to import the modules we're interested in, inspect the signatures of the callable objects found therein and emit a JSON based output (called pgzero_api.json). (adafruit_api.py does the same for CircuitPython by reading its online documentation.)

The resulting JSON is a list of JSON objects containing three attributes:

  • name -- the module name + object name.
  • args -- a list of the arguments taken by the callable Python object being described.
  • description -- the docstring associated with the Python object.

Here's an example of such an object from the emitted pgzero_api.json file:

{
    "description": "Interface to the screen.",
    "name": "screen.Screen",
    "args": [
        "surface"
    ]
}

Given such JSON serialised data, the mkapi.py command will take such a file as input and emit to stdout a list of strings for the API that conform to Scintilla's protocol to be used by autocomplete and call-tips.

In the case of the Pygame Zero mode, the output from the mkapi.py command ended up in PYGAMEZERO_APIS. The list itself is in the plugin's nu_pygamezero/api/pygamezero.py file, and the __init__.py found therein exposes it via the __all__ list. (CircuitPython's is ADAFRUIT_APIS, in nu_circuitpython/api/adafruit.py.)

The mode's api method then returns the APIs that a user of the mode may use: the entries it gets from its host, plus its own. A mode whose programs run in Python 3 starts from self.host.python_apis() (Python's built-ins and standard library); a MicroPython-family mode starts from self.host.shared_apis() (just what every Python has):

from .api import PYGAMEZERO_APIS

... later in the PyGameZeroMode class ...

def api(self):
    return self.host.python_apis() + PYGAMEZERO_APIS

... and in the CircuitPythonMode class ...

def api(self):
    return self.host.shared_apis() + ADAFRUIT_APIS

With these relatively simple steps, it's possible to create quite powerful modes. Most importantly, taking a look at the bundled plugins in plugins/ will reveal how to do most of the things you'll need.

However, there is one final aspect of creating a mode that we need to address.

docs.title: Unit Test the Mode
docs.text:
We will not accept any new modes without 100% unit test coverage.

A bundled plugin keeps its tests in plugins/<name>/tests, where they run with Nu's own (each bundled plugin's tests show how to test a mode through a mock Host).

Please read the guide about tests for how Nu is tested and the various expectations we have when it comes to writing tests.

If you are unsure about the best way to go about testing your mode please feel free to ask for help. We would much rather get a pull request for a "spike" (draft) version of a new mode and work with the original author on testing the code, than have no pull request at all.

If in doubt, ask. We're a friendly bunch and contributing is easy.

docs.title: Packaging Nu
docs.text:
Our target users (beginner programmers and those who support them) may not be confident with installing software, so obtaining and setting up Nu needs to be as simple as possible — and producing the installers needs to be automatic, so cutting a release doesn't depend on one volunteer's time.

The native installers are built with Briefcase (part of the BeeWare suite), which replaced upstream Mu's pup pipeline in Phase 4 (see TODO.md). A single definition in pyproject.toml's [tool.briefcase] drives all three platforms:

OS Format CI runner Windows .msi windows-latest macOS zipped .app (ad-hoc signed) macos-latest (Apple Silicon) Linux .AppImage ubuntu-latest

docs.title: Bundled plugins: the uv workspace
docs.text:
The repo is a uv workspace ([tool.uv.workspace] members = ["plugins/*"] in pyproject.toml). Each bundled plugin is its own package under plugins/<name>/, with its own pyproject.toml, version and mu.plugins entry point, sharing the repo's uv.lock. Today that's nu-circuitpython (plugins/circuitpython) and nu-pygamezero (plugins/pygamezero); plugins/example is a member too, so it's locked and buildable, but it's a template and nothing depends on it.

nu-editor depends on each bundled plugin by name (nu-circuitpython>=0.1, nu-pygamezero>=0.1), and [tool.uv.sources] resolves that name from the workspace, so:

  • Development: uv sync installs the bundled plugins editable into .venv, and Nu finds them through their entry points, the same way it finds a community plugin. The tests for each live in plugins/<name>/tests and run with Nu's.
  • pip from a checkout (as CI's test job does): pip doesn't read [tool.uv.sources], so give it the paths too: pip install ./plugins/circuitpython ./plugins/pygamezero ".[dev]".
  • Installers: Briefcase adds [project.dependencies] to its own requires, so it already asks pip for nu-circuitpython and nu-pygamezero by name. pip finds them as wheels built from the checkout into build/plugin-wheels/, which requirement_installer_args (--find-links) in [tool.briefcase.app.mu] points at; make.py (_build_plugin_wheels) and build.yml build them before briefcase create. The app gets the plugins' entry points, package data (icons, demo assets) and own dependencies (CircuitPython's adafruit-board-toolkit). Don't also list a plugin in requires as a local path ("./plugins/<name>"): pip then fails with "No matching distribution found for nu-", because it meets the name before the path. That broke every installer build from Phase 5c until it was caught by building the macOS app locally (2026-11).
  • Publishing to PyPI: [tool.uv.sources] is uv-only; the built nu-editor sdist/wheel just says Requires-Dist: nu-circuitpython>=0.1 and Requires-Dist: nu-pygamezero>=0.1. So each bundled plugin must be published to PyPI before the nu-editor release that needs it (or pip install nu-editor can't resolve). The order is: nu-circuitpython and nu-pygamezero (in either order: neither depends on the other or on nu-editor), then nu-editor. publish.yml builds all three and uploads them in that order on a release tag, skipping a plugin version PyPI already has (see Publishing to PyPI); make dist and make publish-live (or make publish-test for test PyPI) do the same by hand. Bump a plugin's own version when it changes, independently of Nu's.

docs.title: Opt-in workspace plugins: micro:bit
docs.text:
nu-microbit (plugins/microbit, Phase 6) is a workspace member too, but not a dependency of nu-editor yet: it hasn't been validated on real micro:bits. Instead:

  • nu-editor has an optional extra, microbit = ["nu-microbit>=0.1"], and [tool.uv.sources] resolves nu-microbit from the workspace, so uv sync --all-extras (or --extra microbit) installs it editable in a checkout. A plain uv sync doesn't, and its tests that need the installed entry point skip.
  • CI installs it anyway (./plugins/microbit in test.yml's and docs.yml's pip lines), so its tests and API docs run on every push.
  • It is not one of nu-editor's dependencies or in build.yml's installs and plugin wheels, so the installers don't ship it, and the built nu-editor wheel lists it only as Requires-Dist: nu-microbit>=0.1; extra == "microbit".
  • Its own dependency is mpremote. The MicroPython firmware is not in the package: it's pinned (URL + SHA-256) and downloaded on first use into DATA_DIR/microbit/firmware/.

Promotion (Phase 6c), after the maintainer's hardware pass (the checklist in plugins/microbit/README.md): move nu-microbit>=0.1 from the extra to the dependencies, add it to BUNDLED_PLUGINS in make.py and the Makefile (so its wheel is built for Briefcase and published), to loader.BUNDLED_DISTRIBUTIONS and to build.yml's plugin installs and plugin wheels, and publish it to PyPI before that Nu release. To make Flash work offline from a fresh install, the installer build can also put the two pinned .hex files in nu_microbit/firmware/ (the plugin checks there, after the data folder, and verifies them like a download); fetch them in build.yml with their SHA-256s from nu_microbit/firmware.py, never commit them.

docs.title: What the learner's environment gets from plugins
docs.text: A plugin lists the packages its modes need in the learner's environment (where their programs run, not where Nu runs) as an extra called learner-env, e.g. Pygame Zero's learner-env = ["pgzero>=1.2.1", "pygame>=2.6"]. mu.wheels.baseline_packages() is the core's own list (ipykernel) plus the learner-env requirements of every installed distribution with a mu.plugins entry point, read from package metadata without importing the plugin. That's what goes into the offline wheelhouse and what a new learner environment is built with.

docs.title: Building installers (Briefcase)
docs.text:
CI is the release path: .github/workflows/build.yml builds one OS per job and uploads the installer as a downloadable artifact. Trigger it from the GitHub Actions tab ("Build installers" → Run workflow) and download the artifact for your OS from the run. Pushing a v* tag also builds all three and publishes a GitHub Release with the installers attached. Release tags are plain numeric vX.Y.Z (Windows MSI versions can't carry a pre-release segment). See Release process.

Briefcase is pinned per platform in build.yml: Windows uses 0.4.5, whose MSI template replaces an installed older (or same-version) Nu instead of installing alongside it; macOS and Linux stay on 0.4.2 because 0.4.5 breaks the AppImage. The MSI's UpgradeCode is pinned as guid in pyproject.toml — never change it, or Windows will stop treating new installers as upgrades.

Locally (inside a virtual environment that has pip, with the package extra: uv sync --extra package, or with pip pip install -e ./plugins/circuitpython -e ./plugins/pygamezero -e ".[package]"):

$ make win64     # 64-bit Windows MSI
$ make macos     # macOS .app/.dmg (ad-hoc signed)
$ make linux     # Linux AppImage

Each target fetches the offline baseline wheels, builds the bundled plugins' wheels and runs the Briefcase create → build → package cycle (see make.py). The build is mostly self-driving once the build tools are present (Briefcase fetches WiX for the Windows MSI on demand).

docs.title: What ships inside the app
docs.text:
• The editor (mu) plus its third-party dependencies (PyQt6, etc.), installed into the bundle by Briefcase from [tool.briefcase.app.mu].requires.
  • A pinned uv binary — it rides in via the PyPI uv wheel, and find_uv() locates it at runtime through uv.find_uv_bin() (no PATH or MU_UV needed in the packaged app). It's preferred to a uv on the learner's PATH, which may be older than Nu needs (uv>=0.9.8); MU_UV still overrides both.
  • The bundled plugins (plugins/pygamezero, plugins/circuitpython), installed by Briefcase from wheels built from the checkout (build/plugin-wheels/, see above).
  • The baseline wheels zip (mu/wheels/<version>.zip), so the learner's baseline packages install without the network: the core's (ipykernel) plus the bundled plugins' learner-env packages (Pygame Zero's pgzero and pygame; CircuitPython declares none, as its code runs on the board).
  • A relocatable CPython (the python-build-standalone build uv itself would install, matching the app's Python X.Y and the runner's platform) plus a pip wheel, in mu/wheels/python/.

python -m mu.wheels --package fetches all three before packaging (it needs uv installed, to look up the CPython download, and the bundled plugins installed, to read their learner-env needs; CI's build job installs them with pip install --no-deps ./plugins/circuitpython ./plugins/pygamezero, which needs no PyQt6).

At first launch Nu extracts the bundled CPython into its data directory (a stable, writable path: the app bundle may be read-only, and an AppImage is mounted somewhere new on every launch) and creates the learner's environment with uv venv --python <that interpreter> --seed --no-index --find-links mu/wheels/python. Nothing touches the network. The app's own interpreter can't be the base: in a packaged app sys.executable is Briefcase's launcher stub, which uv can't inspect. In a dev checkout without the bundled CPython, Nu falls back to uv venv --python <X.Y>, letting uv find or download a matching Python.

This adds about 25 MB to each installer.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text: CI builds are unsigned (macOS uses an ad-hoc signature). Users will see a SmartScreen (Windows) or Gatekeeper (macOS) warning until code-signing secrets (Authenticode / Apple notarization) are wired into build.yml — tracked as a follow-up in TODO.md (Phase 4d).

docs.title: Linux desktop integration
docs.text:
Briefcase generates the AppImage's Linux .desktop entry itself, from formal_name and description in pyproject.toml, named after the app id: bundle + app name, i.e. org.kovir.mu.desktop. (Briefcase's AppImage template ships no AppStream metainfo; add one only if we target software centres.) mu/app.py passes the same id to QApplication.setDesktopFileName() so the running window (the Wayland app id) matches the installed .desktop file, which keeps the taskbar icon and window grouping working. If bundle or the app key ever changes, update that call to match.

The pre-Briefcase hand-written metadata (conf/) and the upstream Debian packaging (debian/) were removed along with the pup pipeline (Phase 4e).

docs.title: Writing a Nu plugin
docs.text:
Status: working, but early

Nu loads plugins at startup, both installed packages and files in the plugins folder (Phases 5a and 5b in TODO.md), CircuitPython and Pygame Zero ship as plugins (5c), the Plugins tab lists them and switches them on and off (5e), and micro:bit is back as an opt-in plugin (Phase 6, see The BBC micro:bit). Learners add plugins from PyPI or a wheel file on the Plugins tab, installers included (5d, see Adding a plugin). The API is at version 0.6, so it can still change between releases.

docs.title: Managing plugins
docs.text:
This part is for learners and teachers; the rest of the page is for people writing plugins.

Click the cog in the bottom-right corner of Nu's window and choose the Plugins tab. It lists every plugin Nu found when it started:

Column What it shows On Tick to switch the plugin on, untick to switch it off. Plugin Its name. Hover over it to see what it adds. From Bundled with Nu (it comes with Nu: CircuitPython and Pygame Zero), Installed package (installed into the Python that Nu runs from, e.g. micro:bit while it's opt-in), Added by you (added with Add a plugin… or Add from a file…), or Plugins folder (a file or folder put in Nu's plugins folder). Hover over it for the exact package or file. Status On, Off, Couldn't load, Switched off after errors; see the log, or Removed; gone when you restart Nu. Modes The modes it adds to the mode picker.

Click a plugin to see more about it under the list. If it couldn't load, there's a plain sentence saying why (for example It has an error in its code, so Nu couldn't start it), then the error itself, with a Copy button so you can send it to whoever wrote the plugin.

Switching a plugin off, or back on. Untick it and click OK. Bundled plugins can be switched off too: a class that only uses Python 3 can take CircuitPython and Pygame Zero out of the mode picker. Changes take effect the next time you start Nu; until then the plugin keeps working, and the tab says On until you restart Nu. A switched-off plugin isn't loaded at all.

Adding a plugin. Click Add a plugin… and type its package name, or Add from a file… for a .whl file; see Adding a plugin below. A plugin that's a single .py file (or a folder) goes in the plugins folder instead: click Open plugins folder, put it there, and restart Nu.

When a plugin keeps failing, Nu tells you each time and carries on. After three errors it offers to switch the plugin off; if you agree, the Plugins tab shows it as Switched off after errors; see the log from the next start, and the errors are on the Current Log tab. Tick it to give it another go.

Only add plugins you trust. A plugin is Python code that runs inside Nu, with the same access to your computer as Nu itself: it can read and change your files, like any program you install. Nu can't check what a plugin does.

How to write a plugin on the tab opens this page.

docs.title: Adding a plugin
docs.text:
From PyPI. Click Add a plugin… and type the name of the plugin's package, for example nu-microbit (the plugin's web page says what it is). Nu asks PyPI about it and shows what the package says about itself: its summary, author, web page and latest version. Check it's the one you meant: anyone can put a package on PyPI, and names can look alike. Under that are the trust note and the exact commands Nu will run, such as

uv venv --python <Nu's own Python> <Nu's data folder>/plugin-env
uv pip install --python <Nu's data folder>/plugin-env/bin/python --excludes <Nu's data folder>/plugin-env/nu-provides.txt nu-microbit

Click Add it: the commands run in a progress window, their output streaming in, and they're listed under What Nu Ran afterwards. The plugin loads the next time you start Nu; until then the tab lists it under When you restart Nu.

Only a package name is accepted (nu-microbit, or with a version such as nu-microbit>=0.2): not a web address, a file path or an option for uv.

From a file (no internet). A teacher can download a plugin's wheel (a .whl file) once and share it. Add from a file… asks for the file, shows its name and version, and installs it the same way. A newer file of a plugin you added replaces it.

What Nu checks. After installing, Nu reads the new package's details (without running it) and removes it again, saying why, if

  • it isn't a Nu plugin (it doesn't declare a mu.plugins entry point), or
  • it needs a version of a package Nu already has (PyQt6, say) that isn't the one Nu has.

A package Nu already has (a bundled plugin, or PyQt6) can't be added, and one you've already added is updated with Update instead.

Packages for your programs. If the plugin lists packages your programs need (its learner-env extra), Nu installs them into your Python environment straight away, with uv pip install --python <your environment's Python> …, also shown in the window and under What Nu Ran. If there's no environment yet, they're added when Nu makes it.

Updating and removing. Pick a plugin you added and click Update to get its latest version from PyPI (uv pip install --upgrade …; one added from a file is updated by adding a newer file), or Remove to uninstall it (uv pip uninstall …, after asking). Both take effect at the next start. Bundled plugins, installed packages and plugins-folder plugins have neither button: switch them off, or delete the file.

After a Nu upgrade. Plugins you added are built for the Python Nu runs on. If a new Nu moves to a new Python (3.11 to 3.12, say), they're not loaded (the log says why), and the Plugins tab says so, with a Reinstall my plugins button: it makes the plugin environment again with Nu's new Python and adds every plugin you'd added. One added from a file that's no longer there is reported, and you can add it again.

Limits, for now:

  • Removing a plugin leaves the packages it needed in the plugin environment. They're harmless (only a package with a mu.plugins entry point is loaded) and Reinstall my plugins starts the environment afresh. The packages it added to your Python environment stay too, since your programs may use them.
  • Installing by name needs the internet; the installers don't carry any plugins besides the bundled ones. Add from a file… works offline.
  • There's no list of recommended plugins to choose from, and no checking beyond the above: you choose which plugins to trust.
  • If a plugin you added and one in the plugins folder have the same id, the one you added wins (as installed packages always do).
  • A plugin in the plugins folder can't list packages for your programs (it has no package details); package it to do that.

For teachers: where the choice is kept

Nu keeps the ids of switched-off plugins (the Id in a plugin's details) in its settings.json, in the same data folder as plugins/, and saves it as soon as you click OK:

{
  "disabled_plugins": ["pygamezero"]
}

To prepare several computers, you can write that file yourself while Nu is closed. plugins_switched_off_after_errors lists the plugins Nu switched off because they kept failing; leave it out.

docs.title: Why plugins
docs.text:
Nu is shrinking to a lean core — text editing, the REPL, the debugger, settings, the uv-managed environment, and a plugin host. Everything else — CircuitPython, Pygame Zero, micro:bit, and whatever the community builds — becomes a plugin: an installable package that registers itself with the core and contributes one or more modes (and, over time, panes, menu items, and API metadata for autocomplete).

This page is the contract for plugin authors. For the surrounding rationale and roadmap, see Phase 5 (architecture) and Phase 6 (the micro:bit plugin) in TODO.md.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: Term Meaning Core The always-present editor: editing, REPL, debugger, settings, the uv environment, and the plugin host. Ships the built-in Python 3 + Debugger modes. Plugin An installable package that extends the core through the public mu.plugin API. Mode The primary thing a plugin contributes — a named, icon-bearing "personality" that adds toolbar buttons, autocomplete APIs, a workspace directory, etc. (today's BaseMode). Host The stable façade the core hands a plugin at load time — the only supported way to touch the editor. Bundled plugin A first-party plugin shipped and enabled by default. Today: CircuitPython (plugins/circuitpython) and Pygame Zero (plugins/pygamezero). micro:bit follows (Phase 6).

docs.title: How a plugin is discovered
docs.text:
Nu looks for plugins once, at startup, in two places. Changes take effect the next time Nu starts.

  1. Installed packages. Any package installed in the environment Nu runs from, or added by the learner into the plugin environment (see below), that declares a mu.plugins entry point (see The entry point). Its id is the entry point's name.

  2. The plugins folder, for local plugins that aren't packaged:

    System Folder Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\python\mu\plugins macOS ~/Library/Application Support/mu/plugins Linux ~/.local/share/mu/plugins

    Nu creates the folder if it's missing. Each name.py file, or name/ folder with an __init__.py, is one plugin with id name. The plugin is the module's PLUGIN attribute if it sets one; otherwise the module must define exactly one Plugin subclass. A plugin folder imports its own files with relative imports (from .modes import MyMode). Names starting with . or _ are ignored. A name that matches an installed module (json.py, say) is refused rather than allowed to replace that module.

Installed packages are found first. If a folder plugin has the same id as an installed one, the folder plugin is skipped.

Installers and installed packages

In the Windows, macOS and Linux installers, Nu runs from its own bundled environment, which can't be installed into (it's read-only, and changing it would break the app's signature and its upgrades). So plugins the learner adds (see Adding a plugin) go into a plugin environment of their own, plugin-env in Nu's data folder, made with Nu's own Python so their compiled code matches the process that imports them. At startup, before plugins are discovered, its site-packages goes on sys.path with site.addsitedir (so .pth files work), after Nu's own entries, so Nu's packages (PyQt6 above all) always win. It's left off, with the reason in the log, if it was made with another Python.

plugin-env.json, next to it, records that Python and what the learner added (the name as typed, or the wheel file), so Reinstall my plugins can make it again. Every install passes uv --excludes with a list of every package Nu's own process has (plugin-env/nu-provides.txt), so the plugin environment never gets a second PyQt6, QScintilla or nu-editor; afterwards Nu checks the plugin's own requirements on those packages against the versions Nu has.

In a development checkout (uv pip install -e path/to/plugin) or a pip install nu-editor, installing into Nu's environment works too.

docs.title: When a plugin is skipped
docs.text:
Nu logs the reason, shows it on the Plugins tab (Couldn't load, with the details), and starts without the plugin if it:

  • is switched off;
  • has the same id as a plugin already found;
  • fails to import, including calling sys.exit() while importing;
  • declares a missing or incompatible api_version; or
  • raises an error in register.

Any modes it registered before failing are removed again. An unnamed plugin (one that doesn't set name) is called by its id.

docs.title: When a plugin has an error
docs.text:
Once loaded, a plugin's errors don't crash Nu. That covers errors in the mode methods Nu calls (activate, actions, api, workspace_dir, stop, …) and in anything Qt calls for the plugin: button handlers, timers and signal handlers. For each error:

  • The learner sees a dialog naming the plugin, with the error for its author. Nu keeps running.
  • The log gets the full traceback. An identical repeat gets a one-line entry instead.
  • Nu falls back to something safe when it was calling the mode: api() and actions() give an empty list, workspace_dir() the usual workspace, and the rest give None.
  • Dialogs are rate limited. Further errors within 30 seconds, or while a dialog is open, go to the status bar instead, so a failing timer can't bury the learner in dialogs.
  • A plugin that keeps failing (3 errors) is offered to be switched off. If the learner agrees, it isn't loaded the next time Nu starts, and the Plugins tab says it was switched off after errors. Switching it back on there starts the count afresh.

An error counts as the plugin's when the plugin's own modules appear in the traceback, or when core code was running on one of its modes (for example MicroPythonMode code it inherits).

Threads are covered too. If an error ends a thread your plugin started (a threading.Thread, a QThread or a QRunnable), it's reported the same way, with the thread's name in the log. The dialog itself is always shown from Nu's main thread, so it's safe. Errors in threads that aren't a plugin's go to Nu's log as well. As ever, never touch Qt widgets from your own threads: send a signal to the main thread instead.

For a problem the learner can fix, raise PluginError instead. Nu shows your message as is, and doesn't count it against the plugin:

from mu.plugin import PluginError

def flash(self, event=None):
    if not self.find_devices():
        raise PluginError(
            "Plug in your micro:bit first.",
            "Use a USB cable that carries data, not just power.",
        )

docs.title: Switching a plugin off
docs.text: Learners do it on the Plugins tab (see Managing plugins), which keeps the plugin's id in disabled_plugins in Nu's settings.json. A switched-off plugin isn't even imported, so its register isn't called.

docs.title: The API
docs.text:
Everything a plugin needs is imported from mu.plugin. Nothing else in mu is public: mu.modes, mu.logic and mu.interface can change in any release.

Name What it is PLUGIN_API_VERSION The API version this Nu provides, e.g. "0.6". Plugin Base class for a plugin. ModePlugin A Plugin that registers one or more modes for you. Mode Base class for a mode (today's BaseMode). MicroPythonMode A Mode with serial REPL, plotter and board detection, for MicroPython devices. Device A board a MicroPythonMode found: what its compatible_board(port) returns, and find_devices() lists. (0.3) Host What a plugin is handed: the supported way to reach the editor. PluginSettings A plugin's own persisted settings (from Host.settings). PluginError Raise it for a problem the learner can fix; Nu shows the message (see When a plugin has an error). check_compatible The version check Host applies when loading a plugin.

docs.title: The entry point
docs.text:
A packaged plugin advertises itself in its pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."mu.plugins"]
microbit = "nu_microbit:MicrobitPlugin"

The value points at a Plugin subclass, a Plugin instance, or a function that returns one.

docs.title: Versioning: api_version
docs.text:
Each plugin declares the PLUGIN_API_VERSION it was written against, as a literal string. When loading it, the host compares that with its own version:

  • Same MAJOR, and a MINOR no newer than Nu's: the plugin loads.
  • While MAJOR is 0: the MINOR must match exactly, because 0.x releases may break the API.
  • Anything else, or a missing/malformed api_version: the plugin is logged and skipped. Nu carries on without it.

docs.title: Plugin
docs.text:
from mu.plugin import Plugin

class MyPlugin(Plugin):
    name = "My Plugin"
    description = "Adds My mode, for doing my thing."
    api_version = "0.6"

    def register(self, host):
        """Called once when the plugin loads. Do all wiring here, through
        `host`."""

    def unregister(self, host):
        """Optional. Called when the plugin unloads. Modes it registered are
        removed for you; undo anything else here."""

name and description (0.4) are what the Plugins tab shows: keep the description to one sentence saying what the plugin adds. Both are optional; a plugin without a name is called by its id. A plugin that isn't imported (it's switched off, or failed to import) is shown with what its package says about itself, read without importing it: its distribution name and its summary (description in pyproject.toml), so make that summary the same sentence. A drop-in plugin has no package, so it's shown by its id.

If register raises, the plugin is logged and skipped, and any modes it had already registered are removed. A broken plugin never stops Nu starting.

For the common case of a plugin that only adds modes, use ModePlugin:

from mu.plugin import ModePlugin

class MicrobitPlugin(ModePlugin):
    name = "micro:bit"
    description = "Adds micro:bit mode, for the BBC micro:bit."
    api_version = "0.6"
    mode = MicrobitMode          # or: modes = (ModeA, ModeB)
    # Optional: the folder of icons the modes use (see "Icons and images").
    images = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "images")

docs.title: Mode
docs.text:
Mode is the mode base class the built-in modes use (see Modes). Set the class attributes and override the methods you need:

from mu.plugin import Mode

class MicrobitMode(Mode):
    name = "micro:bit"             # shown in the mode picker
    short_name = "microbit"        # stable, unique id (settings and session keys)
    description = "Write MicroPython for the BBC micro:bit."
    icon = "microbit"              # an image name: Nu's, or your plugin's

    def actions(self):
        """Toolbar buttons."""
        return [
            {
                "name": "microbit-flash",   # also its icon and button id
                "display_name": "Flash",
                "description": "Flash your code to the micro:bit.",
                "handler": self.flash,
                "shortcut": "F3",
            },
        ]

    def api(self):
        """Autocomplete and call tip entries."""
        return MICROBIT_APIS

    # Optional hooks: activate(), deactivate(), stop(), workspace_dir(),
    # ensure_workspace_assets(workspace_dir)

Two more things a mode can declare (new in 0.2):

Member Meaning star_imports = {} A dict mapping a module to the names its import * brings in (the micro:bit lists from microbit import *'s). Check reads such an import as naming them, so it can still spot undefined names. uses_user_environment = False Set it to True if the mode runs the learner's programs in Nu's Python environment (as Python 3 and Pygame Zero do). The admin dialog then shows that environment's variables and third-party packages. ensure_workspace_assets(workspace_dir) Called the first time the mode is used each time Nu runs (including the mode Nu starts in), once the workspace exists; a mode the learner doesn't use leaves the workspace alone. Put what the mode needs there (Pygame Zero makes its images, fonts, sounds and music folders and copies in demo files). Leave anything already there alone. Errors are reported like any other plugin error and don't stop Nu starting.

Inside a mode, self.host is the Host that registered it. Use it rather than self.editor and self.view, which are the internal objects and are not part of the API.

For a MicroPython board, subclass MicroPythonMode instead and list the boards in valid_boards as (vid, pid, manufacturer, board_name) tuples. Nu then detects the board when it's plugged in and offers to switch to your mode. If matching on USB ids isn't enough, override compatible_board(port) (port is a Qt QSerialPortInfo): return a Device for a port that is your board, or None. Build it as Device(vid, pid, port_path, serial_number, manufacturer, self.name, self.short_name, board_name); self.port_path(port.portName()) gives the path. CircuitPython does this, asking adafruit-board-toolkit which ports are CircuitPython REPLs.

MicroPythonMode brings toggle_repl and toggle_plotter, handlers for a Serial and a Plotter button that connect to the board Nu has detected (and tell the learner if there's none). Offer the Plotter only if self.host.plotter_available.

docs.title: Host
docs.text:
Method Does register_mode(mode_class) Create the mode and add it to the editor. Its short_name must be unique. Returns the mode. show_message(message, information=None, icon=None) Show a modal message. icon is "NoIcon", "Question", "Information", "Warning" (the default) or "Critical". confirm(message, information=None, icon=None) Ask OK/Cancel; returns True for OK. show_status(message, duration=5) Show a message in the status bar for duration seconds. current_text() The current tab's text, or None if no tab is open. current_path() The current tab's file path, or None. workspace_dir() The learner's workspace directory. open_directory(path) Open path in the system file manager. save_current() Save the current tab, asking for a name if it has none. Returns its path, or None if there's no tab or the learner cancelled. (0.2) run_program(path, python_args=None, interactive=False) Run the Python program at path as the Run button does: in the learner's environment, with their environment variables, from the program's folder, output in the output pane. python_args go before the program (e.g. ["-m", "pgzero"]). Returns True if it started. (0.2) stop_program() Stop the program run_program started and close its pane. (0.2) update_action(name, display_name=None, description=None, icon=None) Change the current mode's toolbar button name: label, tooltip and/or icon. Raises ValueError if there's no such button. (0.2) register_images(directory) Make the images in directory available by name (see below). (0.2) python_apis() The Python 3 mode's autocomplete entries, as a new list to add yours to. (0.2) shared_apis() The autocomplete entries every Python has, MicroPython and CircuitPython included (built-ins, str/list/dict methods), as a new list: what a board mode's api() builds on. (0.3) plotter_available True if Nu can show the plotter (the optional Qt Charts package is installed). A property. (0.3) current_device The board picked in the device selector (a Device), or None. A property; use it instead of self.editor.current_device. (0.5) data_dir(name) A folder of your plugin's own in Nu's data folder, <data folder>/<name>, made if missing (name is a plain folder name, normally your plugin's id). For downloads and caches, not the learner's work. (0.5) log_command(argv, cwd=None, note=None) Add a command to What Nu Ran (and Nu's log), next to uv's: argv as the learner could type it, note for anything they should know (e.g. "Nu did this through mpremote's Python API"). Returns a record: call add_output(text) as output arrives and finish(exit_code, output=None) when done (0 for success). Safe from any thread. (0.5) add_pane(widget, title, area="bottom") Dock widget, your own Qt widget (PyQt6 is Nu's, so you can import it), in Nu's window with title, at "bottom", "left" or "right", as the REPL and plotter are docked. If the widget has a set_theme(theme) method, it's called with "day", "night" or "contrast" now and whenever the theme changes. Returns a handle for remove_pane. The pane belongs to the current mode: Nu removes it when the learner leaves the mode or your plugin unloads. (0.6) remove_pane(pane) Take away a pane add_pane docked; nothing happens if it's already gone. (0.6) open_file(path) Open the file at path in a tab, as if the learner had loaded it (or go to its tab). (0.6) settings(namespace) A PluginSettings with get(key, default=None) and set(key, value). Values are saved with the user's settings under plugins.<namespace> and must be JSON-serialisable. logger(name) A logger writing to Nu's log as mu.plugins.<name>. api_version The PLUGIN_API_VERSION this Nu provides.

The core uses load_plugin, unload_plugin, modes, plugins, plugin_records, describe_plugins, set_plugin_enabled and plugins_folder, and for adding plugins plugin_env_status, plugin_environment_state, check_plugin_name, check_plugin_file, look_up_plugin, add_plugin, update_plugin, remove_plugin and reinstall_plugins (all but the first four for the Plugins tab); plugins shouldn't need them, and they're not part of the versioned API.

docs.title: Icons and images
docs.text:
A mode's icon, each action's name and update_action(icon=...) are image names: a file name.svg or name.png. Nu looks in its own images first, then in folders plugins have registered, in the order they were registered. A plugin registers its folder by setting ModePlugin.images (registered before its modes) or calling host.register_images(directory); it's removed again when the plugin unloads. The same names work in a theme stylesheet's images: URLs.

An action's name is also its toolbar button's id, so it has to be unique anyway. Image names must be unique too: if your folder has an image named like one Nu or an already-loaded plugin has (whatever the extension), register_images raises ValueError naming it, so your plugin fails to register and is skipped, with the reason in the log. Prefix your image names with your plugin's name (as plugins/example does: example-mode, example-count) so a later Nu can't take a name you use. Your mode can still use Nu's own icons by name (Pygame Zero uses Nu's stop).

docs.title: Packages for the learner's environment
docs.text:
The learner's programs run in Nu's own Python environment for them, not the one Nu runs from. If your mode needs packages there (Pygame Zero needs pgzero and pygame), list them as an extra called learner-env in your pyproject.toml:

[project.optional-dependencies]
learner-env = ["pgzero>=1.2.1", "pygame>=2.6"]

Nu reads it from your package's metadata, without importing your plugin, so it counts even while your plugin is switched off. These packages are installed with Nu's own when the learner's environment is built (on first run, and when Nu is upgraded), and bundled plugins' wheels ship in the installers so that works offline. When a learner adds your plugin from the Plugins tab, they're installed into their existing environment straight away (see Adding a plugin). Drop-in plugins (which have no package metadata) can't declare any.

docs.title: Not in the API yet
docs.text:
These are planned, and are deliberately left out until a real plugin needs them:

  • Settings pages in the admin dialog.
  • Translations for plugins. Bundled plugins use Nu's own message catalog (their strings are extracted with Nu's); a community plugin's strings aren't translated yet.

docs.title: What changed in 0.6
docs.text: 0.6 adds panes, for micro:bit's Files pane: Host.add_pane and Host.remove_pane (see the micro:bit Files pane), and Host.open_file. Nothing was removed, but a 0.5 plugin needs its api_version changed to "0.6".

docs.title: What changed in 0.5
docs.text: 0.5 adds what the micro:bit plugin needs to stay on the API: Host.log_command (so a plugin's equivalent commands show in What Nu Ran, as uv's do), Host.current_device (the selected board, without self.editor) and Host.data_dir (a folder for downloads such as firmware). Nothing was removed, but a 0.4 plugin needs its api_version changed to "0.5".

docs.title: What changed in 0.4
docs.text: 0.4 adds Plugin.description, the sentence the Plugins tab shows under your plugin's name. Nothing was removed, but a 0.3 plugin needs its api_version changed to "0.4".

docs.title: What changed in 0.3
docs.text: 0.3 adds what a MicroPython-family mode needs, so CircuitPython could become a plugin: Device, Host.shared_apis() and Host.plotter_available. Nothing was removed, but a 0.2 plugin needs its api_version changed to "0.3".

docs.title: What changed in 0.2
docs.text: 0.2 adds plugin images (register_images, ModePlugin.images), the mode members uses_user_environment and ensure_workspace_assets, the learner-env extra, and the Host methods save_current, run_program, stop_program, update_action and python_apis. Nothing was removed, but while the API is 0.x a plugin must target the exact minor version, so a 0.1 plugin needs its api_version changed to "0.2" (and is skipped, with the reason logged, until it is).

docs.title: Packaging & distribution
docs.text:
• A plugin is a normal Python distribution: its own pyproject.toml declaring dependencies, the mu.plugins entry point and (optionally) the learner-env extra. Learners add it from the Plugins tab (by name from PyPI, or from its wheel file); it shouldn't list nu-editor as a dependency (Nu leaves it out anyway).
  • Bundled plugins live in this repo under plugins/<name>/ as members of a uv workspace (shared lockfile; independently buildable and publishable). They are also published to PyPI, so they travel the exact same path a third-party plugin does — dogfooding the community story. See Bundled plugins below.
  • Community plugins live in their own repositories and publish independently. A bundled plugin "graduates" to its own repo only once the API is stable and it has a reason to diverge (separate maintainer, release cadence, or licence) — which, because it is already its own package, is a trivial directory move.
  • Licensing: the core is GPLv3. Whether a plugin is a derivative work is the classic murky plugin question; first-party plugins stay GPLv3, and community authors should weigh the API boundary's licence implications.

docs.title: Versioning & compatibility
docs.text:
• The core advertises PLUGIN_API_VERSION; each plugin declares api_version (the rules are under Versioning above).
  • An incompatible plugin is logged and skipped, never a crash. The Plugins tab shows it as Couldn't load, saying it was written for a different version of Nu, with the exact versions in its details.
  • The API is bumped deliberately, with a short compatibility-shim window. It stays at 0.x until the micro:bit plugin (Phase 6) has proven it: 0.5 is what micro:bit needed to be built on the API alone and 0.6 added panes for its Files pane (below); it should reach 1.0 once the plugin has passed its hardware checks.

docs.title: Trust & safety
docs.text: Plugins are arbitrary in-process Python — there is no sandbox. The trust model is the same as pip: you chose to install it. The Plugins tab says so in plain words: a plugin runs inside Nu with the same access to your computer as Nu itself, so only add plugins you trust, as you'd only install programs you trust. Before adding a plugin, Nu shows what PyPI says about it (to help spot a look-alike name) and the real uv commands it will run. (A curated/signed index is a possible future, not a v1 guarantee.) In-process plugins can't be meaningfully sandboxed without a far larger redesign, which is out of scope.

docs.title: The micro:bit Files pane
docs.text:
Upstream Mu's micro:bit mode had a Files pane: the files on the board on one side, the learner's microbit folder on the other. Nu removed the old FileSystemPane (and the frozen microfs behind it) in Phase 1; it came back in API 0.6 as plugin-owned UI driven by mpremote, and is the worked example for panes:

  • The widget (nu_microbit/files_pane.py) is the plugin's own PyQt6 code: two lists and the buttons between them. It only says what the learner asked for, through Qt signals; the mode does it.
  • Docking: the mode calls host.add_pane(pane, "micro:bit Files") and host.remove_pane(handle); Nu removes it anyway when the learner leaves micro:bit mode. A file is opened with host.open_file(path).
  • Talking to the board (nu_microbit/files.py): the same worker pattern as Flash, one job at a time on a QThread, through mpremote's SerialTransport: fs_readfile / fs_writefile to copy each way and fs_rmfile to delete, each logged under What Nu Ran as mpremote connect <port> fs cp :a.py a.py / fs cp a.py :a.py / fs rm :a.py. Listing (fs ls) runs a few lines of its own: mpremote's fs_listdir needs os.ilistdir, which micro:bit MicroPython's flat file system doesn't have (it has os.listdir and os.size).
  • One serial port: the pane, the REPL and Flash all need it, so the REPL and plotter close (and stay off) while the pane is open, and Flash refreshes the pane afterwards.
  • Tests: a fake board with an in-memory file system, as the flash tests fake the board; the hardware checklist in plugins/microbit/README.md.

docs.title: A minimal example
docs.text:
my-nu-plugin/
├── pyproject.toml          # deps + [project.entry-points."mu.plugins"]
└── my_nu_plugin/
    ├── __init__.py         # MyPlugin(ModePlugin) + MyMode(Mode)
    └── images/             # my-plugin-mode.svg, my-plugin-action.svg, ...

A runnable template lives in this repo at plugins/example/: an "Example" mode with its own icons and one button that counts the lines in the current tab and stores a setting. To start a plugin from it:

  1. Copy plugins/example and rename the package (nu_example), the project name, the entry point and the short_name.
  2. Rename the images, keeping your plugin's prefix, and point icon and the actions' names at them.
  3. List anything your mode needs in the learner's environment under learner-env.
  4. Install it into the environment Nu runs from (uv pip install -e path/to/plugin in a checkout) and restart Nu.

plugins/microbit/ is the one for a board that also flashes firmware: a GUI-free state machine run on a QThread, a pinned-and-fetched download, and commands echoed with Host.log_command.

plugins/pygamezero/ is the worked example of a full mode: buttons that toggle, running the learner's program, workspace assets, autocomplete stubs and tests. plugins/circuitpython/ is the one for a board: a MicroPythonMode with its own board detection, the learner's files on the board's drive, Serial and Plotter buttons, and a dependency of its own (adafruit-board-toolkit) in the environment Nu runs from.

docs.title: Bundled plugins
docs.text:
A bundled plugin is an ordinary plugin package that lives in this repo, under plugins/<name>/, and ships with Nu, switched on by default:

  • It's a member of the repo's uv workspace, and nu-editor depends on it, so uv sync installs it (editable) and Nu finds it through its entry point, just as it finds a community plugin. The installers include it as a wheel built from the checkout (see packaging).
  • It imports only mu.plugin, so it can graduate to its own repository by moving the folder.
  • Its tests live in plugins/<name>/tests and run with Nu's (pytest collects tests and plugins; coverage covers both).
  • It uses Nu's message catalog: make translate_begin extracts its strings with the core's.
  • It's published to PyPI before the Nu release that depends on it.

To add one: create plugins/<name>/ (from the template), add "nu-<name>>=<version>" to nu-editor's dependencies and nu-<name> = { workspace = true } to [tool.uv.sources], add its folder to BUNDLED_PLUGINS in make.py and the Makefile and its name to loader.BUNDLED_DISTRIBUTIONS, its source folder to pythonpath in [tool.pytest.ini_options], its package to _TRANSLATE_PLUGIN_PACKAGES in make.py, and its path to the pip installs in .github/workflows/test.yml, docs.yml and build.yml (and to build.yml's plugin wheels and publish.yml's builds), and to mkdocstrings' paths in mkdocs.yml. Then uv lock.

docs.title: In the repo but opt-in: micro:bit
docs.text:
plugins/microbit/ (nu-microbit) is a workspace member like the bundled plugins, with its tests run in CI, but it is not one of nu-editor's dependencies (so the installers don't carry it), and not in loader.BUNDLED_DISTRIBUTIONS, so the Plugins tab shows it as an Installed package. It's installed by nu-editor's microbit extra (uv sync --all-extras in a checkout). Until a plugin has been tried on real hardware, it stays opt-in like this; its README has the checklist. Promoting it (Phase 6c) is the steps above: add it to the dependencies and requires, to BUNDLED_DISTRIBUTIONS and to build.yml's installs, and drop the extra.

If a bundled plugin's mode used to be built in, keep its short_name: saved sessions and the mode setting refer to it. (If the plugin is switched off or missing, Nu asks the learner to pick a mode at startup, as it does for any mode it doesn't know.)

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Modes — the mode concept the plugin Mode formalizes.
  • API reference — generated from the mu.plugin docstrings.
  • TODO.md — Phase 5 (plugin architecture) and Phase 6 (the micro:bit plugin).

docs.title: Publishing to PyPI
docs.text: How Nu gets to PyPI. Nothing is published yet: the workflow is in place, and the one-time setup below is what's left. As of 2026-11-09, the names nu-editor, nu-circuitpython, nu-pygamezero, nu-microbit and nu-example-plugin were all unclaimed.

docs.title: What gets published
docs.text:
Package When Why nu-pygamezero, nu-circuitpython With every release that changes them nu-editor depends on them, so they must be on PyPI first nu-editor Every release Gives pip install nu-editor / pipx install nu-editor as an install route, and plugin authors develop against it nu-microbit Once it is promoted to a bundled plugin (Phase 6c) Doubles as the worked example for community plugin authors

nu-example-plugin is a copy-me template; it isn't published.

The installers don't need PyPI: they carry the bundled plugins as wheels, so a first launch stays offline. PyPI is for pip installs and for the Plugins tab's Add a plugin….

Don't hold names with empty packages

PyPI's name policy (PEP 541) treats empty placeholder packages as name squatting, and PyPI can hand those names to someone else. Publish each plugin only once it has real code.

docs.title: One-time setup: Trusted Publishing
docs.text:
Trusted Publishing lets PyPI accept uploads straight from a GitHub Actions workflow, so there is no API token to store or leak.

  1. pypi.org (2FA required): Account → Publishing → Add a new pending publisher → GitHub. Do this three times, once per project name (nu-editor, nu-pygamezero, nu-circuitpython), each with:

    • Owner: kovirlabs
    • Repository: nu
    • Workflow filename: publish.yml
    • Environment: pypi

    A pending publisher creates the project on its first upload. 2. test.pypi.org (a separate site with its own account): add the same three pending publishers, with environment testpypi. This is what a dry run uploads to. 3. GitHub: repo Settings → Environments: create pypi and add yourself as a required reviewer, so no upload goes out until you approve it. Create testpypi too (no reviewer needed).

When another plugin is ready to publish, add a pending publisher for its project name (same owner, repo, workflow and environment) and add its folder to the build step in publish.yml, and to BUNDLED_PLUGINS in make.py and the Makefile.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
.github/workflows/publish.yml builds the sdist and wheel of nu-editor and of each bundled plugin (the same builds as make dist), runs twine check, and uploads the plugins and then nu-editor. A plugin version the index already has is skipped; nu-editor's version must be new.

  • A release tag (vX.Y.Z) uploads to PyPI, after checking that the tag matches the version in mu/__init__.py. The run waits for your approval in the pypi environment.
  • A manual run (Actions → Publish to PyPI → Run workflow) uploads to TestPyPI by default, or to PyPI if you choose it.

Do a TestPyPI run before the first real release: it exercises the whole path, and it hasn't been run yet.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Pushing a vX.Y.Z tag runs build.yml, which builds the installers and creates the GitHub Release, and publish.yml, which uploads to PyPI once you approve it. Then check the result in a fresh venv:

python -m venv /tmp/nu-check && /tmp/nu-check/bin/pip install nu-editor
/tmp/nu-check/bin/nu-editor

To check a TestPyPI upload the same way, let pip find Nu's dependencies on PyPI:

pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ nu-editor

An uploaded version can never be reused

Once a version is uploaded, that number is taken for good, even if you delete the release. That holds on TestPyPI too, so a second dry run of the same version fails at nu-editor. This matches the numeric-only policy: ship any fix as the next patch.

docs.title: Fallback: manual upload with a token
docs.text:
Create an API token (PyPI → Account → API tokens), then run make publish-live (or make publish-test for TestPyPI). It runs make check, builds everything and uploads in the same order as the workflow.

Use __token__ as the username and the token as the password. Once the project exists, switch to a token scoped to just this project.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: The author name and kovirlabs@kovir.org from pyproject.toml appear publicly on the PyPI page.

docs.title: Release process
docs.text: This is the checklist for cutting a release of Nu. CI builds and publishes the installers, but it doesn't make a release on its own: the checks, the version numbers and the order of publishing are up to whoever cuts it.

docs.title: What CI does
docs.text:
• test.yml runs the tests on Windows, macOS and Linux for every push and pull request (Python 3.11 and 3.14 everywhere, plus 3.12 and 3.13 on Linux).
  • CodeQL scans the code, through GitHub's default setup (configured in the repository's settings, not in a workflow file).
  • docs.yml publishes these docs on every push to master (see the documentation site).
  • build.yml builds the installers with Briefcase (Windows .msi, macOS zipped .app, Linux .AppImage) when run by hand or when a v* tag is pushed. A tag also publishes a GitHub Release with the installers attached. See packaging.
  • publish.yml uploads nu-editor and its bundled plugins to PyPI when a vX.Y.Z tag is pushed (after your approval), or to TestPyPI when run by hand. See Publishing to PyPI.

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text:
Release versions are plain numeric X.Y.Z: no rc/b/dev suffixes. Windows MSI versions must be numeric, and Briefcase strips any suffix, so 2.0.0b3 and 2.0.0 would be the same version to Windows (the 2.0.0 betas all were). To try out a release before publishing it, build the installers from a manual run (below); once a version is tagged, ship fixes as the next patch (2.0.1). The tag is the version with a v in front (v2.0.0).

The version lives in two places, and both must change together:

  1. __version__ in mu/__init__.py: the canonical one, read by hatchling for the wheel and sdist, and shown in Nu's log.
  2. version under [tool.briefcase] in pyproject.toml: Briefcase reads only this literal, and it names the installer files. Bump only the first and the installers come out labelled with the old version.

The bundled plugins (plugins/pygamezero, plugins/circuitpython) have versions of their own, in their own pyproject.toml. Bump a plugin's version when the plugin changes, independently of Nu's.

docs.title: Before the release
docs.text:
• Translations. If user-facing strings changed since the last release, bring every catalogue up to date (make translate_begin LANG=xx_XX then make translate_done LANG=xx_XX for each locale, as in translations), commit the .po and .mo files, and check make translate_status. Give translators time before the release if you can.
  • Autocomplete data. If a mode's API changed (a new Pygame Zero or CircuitPython version, say), regenerate its API stubs with the scripts in utils/ (see modes).
  • Changelog. Make sure CHANGES.md describes what changed since the last release, for learners and teachers as well as developers, and give the section its version and date.
  • Docs. Re-read the pages for learners (Using Nu, Your Python environment, The BBC micro:bit) against what you're releasing, and build the site with uv run --no-sync mkdocs build --strict.
  • Green. make check passes locally and CI is green on master.

docs.title: Check it as a learner would
docs.text:
Do these on Windows, macOS and Linux, from a clean state: delete Nu's data folder (see Your Python environment) and the mu_code folder first. Running from source with throwaway folders (MU_DATA_DIR=... MU_HOME_DIR=... uv run python -m mu) is fine for a first pass; the installers get the same checks after they're built (below).

  • First start: Nu asks for a mode, makes mu_code and the learner's environment (offline too, from an installer), and doesn't ask again on the next start.
  • Files: New, Load and Save behave; a file with a name is autosaved.
  • Python 3: Run a script that uses input(); Run a script with a # /// script block and a dependency (the uv run command is the first line of the output); the REPL opens and toggles off; the Plotter graphs printed tuples.
  • Debugger: with and without breakpoints; add and remove breakpoints while paused; Stop, Continue, Step Over, Step In, Step Out each do what they say, and the variables inspector updates. Quit Nu afterwards: it exits cleanly.
  • Environment: the status bar shows the environment; clicking it opens the Environment tab; adding and removing a package works and shows the command; What Nu Ran lists the commands; making a second environment under Advanced works.
  • Plugins: the Plugins tab lists Pygame Zero and CircuitPython as on; switching one off and restarting removes its mode; switching it back on restores it.
  • Pygame Zero: Play runs an empty file (a blank window) and a working game; Images, Fonts, Sounds and Music open the right folders.
  • CircuitPython (with a board): Nu offers to switch mode when the board is plugged in; saving code.py runs it; Serial shows the board, and Ctrl+C there gives the REPL; the Plotter graphs tuples.
  • micro:bit (opt-in, from source with uv sync --extra microbit, with a board): the checklist in plugins/microbit/README.md.
  • Everywhere: Zoom-in/Zoom-out, Theme cycles the looks, Check marks problems, Tidy reformats, Help opens Using Nu, Ctrl+K toggles comments, Ctrl+F finds; Quit with unsaved work asks first; the cog opens the admin dialog on Current Log.

docs.title: Cutting the release
docs.text:
The bundled plugins go to PyPI before nu-editor. nu-editor's wheel says Requires-Dist: nu-circuitpython>=… and nu-pygamezero>=…, so if a release needs a new plugin version, that version must be on PyPI before nu-editor is, or pip install nu-editor can't resolve (see packaging). publish.yml (and make publish-live) take care of the order:

  1. For each bundled plugin that changed, bump its version (in its own pyproject.toml). (nu-microbit stays unpublished until it's promoted; see packaging.)
  2. Bump Nu's version in both places (above), finish CHANGES.md, and commit.
  3. On that branch, run Build installers by hand (Actions tab → Run workflow → pick the branch). It builds all three installers as downloadable artifacts without publishing anything.
  4. Download each installer from that run and do the learner checks above on real machines: at least current Windows 11 (installing over the previous release, which it should replace: one "Nu Editor" in Apps), current macOS (Apple Silicon) and a current Ubuntu LTS, with a first launch with the network off.
  5. Merge, then push an annotated tag on that commit: git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Nu 2.0.0" then git push origin v2.0.0. build.yml rebuilds the three installers (from the plugins in the repository, not PyPI) and publishes the GitHub Release with them attached. The tag also starts publish.yml, which uploads the two plugins (a version PyPI already has, because the plugin didn't change, is skipped) and then nu-editor to PyPI once you approve the run in the pypi environment. See Publishing to PyPI for the one-time setup, the TestPyPI dry run and the manual fallback (make publish-live).
  6. Check that pip install nu-editor in a fresh virtual environment installs Nu and its plugins and starts.

If the release went out wrong (say, the installers carry the old version): delete the GitHub Release (gh release delete vX.Y.Z --yes) and the tag (locally and on GitHub), fix it, and tag again. build.yml's gh release create fails if a release for that tag still exists.

The installers are currently unsigned (macOS is ad-hoc signed), so learners see a SmartScreen or Gatekeeper warning; say so in the release notes. Signing is tracked in TODO.md (Phase 4d).

docs.title: After the release
docs.text:
• Announce it where Nu's users are, with a link to the release and CHANGES.md.
  • Start a new "unreleased" section at the top of CHANGES.md.
  • Close the issues the release fixed, and answer reports about it at github.com/kovirlabs/nu/issues.

docs.title: Developer Setup
docs.text:
The source code is hosted on GitHub. Clone the repository with:

git clone https://github.com/kovirlabs/nu.git
cd nu

Nu does not and never will use or support Python 2. Nu targets PyQt6 and Python 3.11+ (verified through 3.14).

docs.title: Setting up with uv (recommended)
docs.text:
Nu uses uv to manage its development environment. uv sync downloads a managed CPython, creates a .venv, and installs the project (editable) with its runtime dependencies, including the bundled plugins in plugins/ (the repo is a uv workspace; see packaging):

uv sync                 # runtime deps only
uv sync --extra dev     # + tests, docs, packaging, i18n and lint tooling
uv sync --all-extras    # + everything, including the opt-in micro:bit plugin

Run things through the environment with uv run:

uv run python run.py    # launch Nu
uv run python -m mu     # equivalent
uv run pytest           # run the test suite

Note

The canonical packaging definition lives in pyproject.toml (hatchling backend); setup.py/setup.cfg were retired. The [dev] extra aggregates the [tests], [docs], [package], [i18n] and [lint] extras. [utils] (scrapers under utils/) and [all] are defined separately.

docs.title: Setting up without uv
docs.text:
If you prefer not to use uv, any Python 3.11+ virtual environment (made with the standard venv module) works:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .\.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ./plugins/circuitpython -e ./plugins/pygamezero -e ".[dev]"
pip install -e ./plugins/microbit   # optional: the opt-in micro:bit plugin

pip doesn't know about the uv workspace, so the bundled plugins (which nu-editor depends on) are given as paths.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
uv run pytest

To run them without a display (over SSH, in a container) use Qt's offscreen platform:

QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen LANG=en_GB.utf8 uv run --no-sync pytest -q --basetemp=$HOME/.cache/nu-pytest/bt

The tests never touch your real Nu settings or mu_code folder. See tests for what each part of that command does, the random test order, coverage and how to write a test.

docs.title: Linting and formatting
docs.text:
Nu uses ruff for both linting and formatting (config in pyproject.toml [tool.ruff], wrapping at 88 columns):

uv run --no-sync python -m ruff check     # lint
uv run --no-sync python -m ruff format    # reformat in place

docs.title: Using make
docs.text:
A Makefile (delegating to make.py) wraps the common workflows. Typing make on its own lists the available targets. The most useful are:

make run       - run the local development version of Nu.
make test      - run the test suite.
make coverage  - run the tests with a coverage report.
make lint      - lint with ruff.
make format    - check formatting; `make tidy` reformats in place.
make check     - format + lint + coverage (the pre-commit gate).
make dist      - build sdists and wheels of Nu and its bundled plugins
                 (runs make check first).
make docs      - build the documentation with MkDocs (make docs-serve to preview).
make translate_status - how complete each translation is (see translations).

Note

On Windows there is a make.cmd file that works in a similar way to the make command on Unix-like operating systems (it calls make.py, as the Makefile does).

docs.title: Before submitting
docs.text: Before contributing code please make sure you've read contributing and follow its checklist. We expect everyone participating in the development of Nu to act in accordance with the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Nu's test suite
docs.text:
We have tests so we can make changes with confidence. We use:

  • pytest for the unit tests, with pytest-random-order so tests can't quietly depend on running in a particular order.
  • Coverage (through pytest-cov) to see which lines the tests exercise.
  • ruff to lint and check the formatting (it replaced Mu's PyFlakes, pycodestyle and black). See setup.

All of them come with the dev extra: uv sync --extra dev.

docs.title: Where the tests are
docs.text:
• Nu's core: tests/, mirroring the source tree. The tests for mu/logic.py are in tests/test_logic.py, those for mu/modes/base.py in tests/modes/test_base.py, and so on.
  • Bundled plugins: each plugin keeps its own tests in plugins/<name>/tests (plugins/pygamezero/tests, plugins/circuitpython/tests, plugins/microbit/tests). pyproject.toml lists both places as testpaths, and puts each plugin's source on sys.path, so a plain pytest runs them all against this checkout. The micro:bit plugin is opt-in: without uv sync --extra microbit (or --all-extras) the tests that need its installed entry point are skipped.

The settings live in pyproject.toml under [tool.pytest.ini_options], and shared fixtures in conftest.py at the repository root.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
uv run pytest

or make test (verbose), or make check, the gate to pass before you open a pull request: it checks formatting, lints, and runs the tests with coverage.

docs.title: Headless, the way CI does it
docs.text:
Qt needs a display. Without one (over SSH, in a container, in CI) use Qt's offscreen platform:

QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen LANG=en_GB.utf8 uv run --no-sync pytest -q --basetemp=$HOME/.cache/nu-pytest/bt
  • QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen draws windows in memory instead of on a screen. On a minimal Linux without Mesa, Qt still wants libEGL.so.1: install your distribution's libegl1, or put the library on LD_LIBRARY_PATH.
  • LANG=en_GB.utf8 gives the locale-sensitive tests the language they expect.
  • --no-sync stops uv run re-syncing the environment first (run uv sync yourself when the dependencies change).
  • -q is optional: one line of dots instead of a line per test.
  • --basetemp=... puts pytest's own temporary folders (tmp_path) under a folder you choose (pytest empties it at the start of each run). You need it where /tmp is mounted noexec: one test makes a real environment in its tmp_path and runs its Python.

The whole suite takes under a minute.

docs.title: A single test, and a reproducible order
docs.text:
uv run pytest tests/test_logic.py::test_editor_init

Tests run in a random order by default (addopts = "--random-order", from pytest-random-order). Each run prints its seed at the top (Using --random-order-seed=...): when a failure only happens in one order, repeat it with --random-order-seed=<seed>. To run in file order instead, add --random-order-bucket=none.

Note

-p no:randomly, which you may see in older instructions, switches off a different plugin (pytest-randomly) that Nu doesn't use, so it doesn't stop the shuffling.

docs.title: Your real Nu data is safe
docs.text:
Before anything imports mu, conftest.py points the whole test session at a new temporary folder (removed when the run ends):
